unit.title: Introduction to Electrical Energy and DC Circuits

title: Network-element classifications; R/L/C energy; nodes, branches and loops
summary: Expanded network-element classification; active/passive, unilateral/bilateral, linear/non-linear, lumped/distributed and time-variant/time-invariant elements; added R/L/C energy notes; nodes, branches and closed loops.
transcription_policy: Notebook order and meaning are preserved; grammar, punctuation and awkward English are lightly cleaned for study. Crossed-out corrections are normalized to the final readable wording, and no new theory is added unless explicitly marked as a short clarification.

mapped_topics.label: Circuit elements: resistance, inductance and capacitance

blocks.alt: Notebook-style classification tree of network elements. Active source elements split into voltage and current sources, each independent or dependent; passive sink elements are resistor R, inductor L and capacitor C. A second tree classifies network elements as linear or non-linear, unilateral or bilateral, active or passive, time-variant or time-invariant, and lumped or distributed.
blocks.caption: Class-note redraw · Updated classification of network elements

blocks.text: Elements that can deliver energy are called active elements; in this class-note classification they are sources of energy. Examples: voltage sources and current sources.
Elements that consume energy by absorbing or storing it are called passive elements. Examples: resistor, inductor and capacitor.

A unilateral element has a different voltage-current relationship in the two directions. A semiconductor diode is the example given in class: it conducts readily in one direction and offers very high resistance in the opposite direction.
A bilateral element has the same voltage-current relationship in either direction.
A circuit element is linear when its voltage-current relationship is linear. The class notes list the element relations:
Example: R, L and C elements.
If an element does not satisfy a linear relationship, it is called a non-linear element. Examples given in class: diodes and thermistors.
Elements that are physically separable are called lumped elements. Examples: resistor, inductor and capacitor.

Elements whose parameters are physically distributed along the element are called distributed elements. A transmission line is the example given in class; its resistance, inductance and capacitance are distributed along the line.
If the parameters of network elements do not vary with time, the elements are time-invariant. If the parameters vary with time, they are time-variant.
Class emphasis: normally, networks are considered with linear, time-invariant and lumped elements.

pages.heading: Additions to the R, L and C notes

blocks.text: A resistor consumes electrical energy; it cannot store or deliver energy.
An ideal inductor stores energy when the current through it changes. It does not consume energy; it stores energy.
A capacitor stores energy when the voltage across it changes. A pure capacitor does not consume energy; it stores energy.
A node is a terminal of a branch or an interconnection common to two or more branches of a network. If more than two elements meet at a node, it is called a principal node.
A branch is a direct path joining two nodes of a network. A branch may contain one or more elements connected in series.
A closed loop starts at a node, travels through part of the circuit and returns to the same node without passing through any node more than once.

blocks.alt: Notebook-style circuit illustrating nodes, branches and loops. Nodes 1, 2, 3 and 4 connect six branches: R2 between 1 and 2; L1 between 2 and 3; R1 between 1 and 4; R3 and C1 in series between 2 and 4; R4 between 3 and 4; and V2, R5 and L2 in series between 1 and 3. Loop regions are marked X, Y and Z.
blocks.caption: Class-note redraw · Nodes, branches and closed loops

blocks.text: How to read the drawing: nodes are 1, 2, 3 and 4. The six branches are 12, 23, 14, 24, 34 and 13, and each node connects three branches.
The marked loops are X: 1→2→4→1, Y: 2→3→4→2 and Z: 1→3→2→1. Branch 24 contains \(R_3\) and \(C_1\) in series; branch 13 contains \(V_2\), \(R_5\) and \(L_2\) in series.
